question: Which half of a production agent's traffic can a 1.5B model take over, and how do you know before shipping it?
method: LoRA SFT (r=16, alpha=32, 3 epochs, lr 1e-4, 51 steps), TRL SFTTrainer, on the boring half only
model: offline (no model API key; incumbent is wai.seeded_agent, reward is a program)
metric: pass@1 on a program that reads the trajectory and names policy flaws (ignore_fault, apology, hedging, sycophancy, boilerplate, leak)

grader_trust.note: zero false alarms; under-detects, so pass rates are upper bounds for both arms equally

split.rule: did the tool call fault (known at runtime, costs no model call)
split.rejected_rule: tier on the row; incumbent 0.72 ordinary vs 0.66 rest, intervals overlap

eval.underpowered: boring slice has 23 asks; holdout_size wants 37 for +0.10, so powered for ~+0.15

train.source: incumbent traces the program marked clean, boring half only

cost_line.note: measured throughput, 496 replies per 25.5s on one L40S

verdict: Both slices moved, every interval excludes zero. But the vs-incumbent rows are near-tautological (the incumbent injects flaws at a fixed 35% rate independent of difficulty). The real finding is the untrained base model: 0.670 boring vs 0.298 hard, a 0.37 gap against a 0.039 noise floor, with ignore_fault the dominant failure. Training on the boring half transferred to the hard half it never saw (0.298 -> 0.951), so the split stopped mattering after 24 examples.
caveats: incumbent failures are uniform-random stylistic flaws, not a capability gap; any imitator of the filtered-clean subset wins
boring delta +0.239 clears its 0.237 noise band by 0.002 - a marginal pass
one seed, one training run; noise floor bounds eval noise only
grader tuned on the incumbent phrasings, so it may under-detect novel flaws from the small model, biasing toward the small model
training reward and eval metric are the same program by design
